# blue

> blue is a general-purpose language with a Ruby/Elixir surface that parses to a tatara-lisp tree and runs on a Rust runtime. It has one formatting, rigor where you write it, safety first, and most of its vocabulary in packages called bidamas.

---

Source: `docs/introduction.md`

# blue

```text
████  blue          nord7 → nord8 → nord9 → nord10
────────────────────    teal   cyan   light  deep blue
a Ruby/Elixir surface on tatara-lisp and Rust
```

**blue** is the pleme-io language. You write it like Ruby or Elixir. It
parses to a [tatara-lisp](https://github.com/pleme-io/tatara-lisp) tree,
macros rewrite that tree, and a Rust runtime runs it, not the BEAM. Each
thing has one spelling, and the formatter writes it. Rigor is your choice:
declare nothing and a program is dynamic and fast; annotate one function and
that function is checked. Safety is not a choice: a program reaches the host
only through the capabilities it is given. The standard library is a set of
packages called bidamas, and one `Bluefile` says how a project is built,
tested, documented and shipped.

The philosophy is two axes
([`theory/BLUE.md`](https://github.com/pleme-io/theory/blob/main/BLUE.md) §0).
**Form has no choices:** there is one short, distinct way to write each
thing, every larger form is built from smaller ones, and every tool and gate
enforces it. **Rigor has every choice:** a program is as strict as you write
it, where you write it, and pays for nothing else. Every blue word (bidama,
waku, mondou, the blueshift) maps to the concept you already know in
[the glossary](docs/GLOSSARY.md).

A file is a program, a library and its tests at once:

```blue file=words.b
@doc """
shout: The text in capitals, with an exclamation mark.

    shout("olá") #=> "OLÁ!"
"""
def shout(text: String) -> String
  "#{upcase(text)}!"
end

def main()
  write_stdout(unlines([join(map(shout, argv), " ")]))
end

test "shout raises its voice and keeps the text"
  assert shout("oi") == "OI!"
  assert shout("") == "!"
end
```

```console
$ blue words.b olá mundo
OLÁ! MUNDO!
$ blue test words.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

The example in the `@doc` is the second test: `blue test` runs it beside the
`test` block, so a documented example cannot drift from the code.

## The blueshift

The blueshift is how far a program has moved from dynamic toward checked.
You move it one definition at a time. Here `add` has no annotation, so
nothing analyses it. `fact` is annotated, so the checker proves it:

```blue file=shift.b
def add(a, b)
  a + b
end

def fact(n: Int) -> Int
  if n < 2
    1
  else
    n * fact(n - 1)
  end
end
```

`blue check` prints what the check cost, so the claim is a measurement:

```console
$ blue check shift.b
typed declarations: 1
nodes analysed:     11
seams:              0
names resolved:     11
waived:             0
```

`blue shift` names the rung the file stands on and what holds it back:

```console
$ blue shift shift.b
██░░ annotated  (1/2 typed, 11 nodes analysed)
some declarations are typed; untyped ones are unchecked

  · untyped declaration      `add` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
  → type annotation          `fact` is annotated, so it is checked
```

The language server closes the gap for you: on a loose definition it offers a
code action that writes the types its calls showed.

## Safety first

Every effect outside the program is a capability: `process`, `filesystem`,
`environment`, `clock`, `network` or `entropy`. `--allow` holds a run to the
ones you name, and the check stage refuses the program before it runs when it
writes a host name outside them:

```blue file=peek.b
def main()
  write_stdout(read_file("words.b"))
end
```

```console fails
$ blue --allow none peek.b
refused: `read_file` reaches the host (filesystem), which this run does not allow; pass --allow filesystem to grant it
```

A script states its capabilities in its shebang,
`#!/usr/bin/env -S blue --allow filesystem`. A project states them once in its
`Bluefile`: `allow` is the ceiling of the whole program, `reach` is the floor
each package needs, and `blue lock` refuses a package whose floor does not fit
under the ceiling. `virtualize` binds a capability to a pure provider, such as
a stepped clock, a seeded random source or an in-memory file tree, for the
whole program or only for the packages you name. An evaluation session
(`eval`, `repl`, `serve`) is pure unless you start it with `--allow`. Every
Rust guarantee, the blue gate that matches it and its off switch are in
[Safety first](docs/SAFETY.md).

## What ships

| Battery | What you get | Read |
|---|---|---|
| The language | macros as term rewriting, with bounded expansion; errors raised and rescued by kind, or returned as refusals; OTP-style processes with private environments, copy-on-send and supervised restarts | [the reference](docs/REFERENCE.md), [the agent guide](AGENTS.md) |
| Tests | `test` blocks beside the code, a doctest in every `@doc`, coverage, mutation testing, and a conformance suite every evaluator must pass | [Testing](docs/TESTING.md), [the spec](spec/README.md) |
| Tools | one formatter; a check stage whose rules carry their own fixes; a language server with hover, completion, definitions, references, rename, signature help, semantic tokens, inlay hints and code actions; a REPL; `watch`, `profile`, `trace` and code queries | [Diagnostics](docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md) |
| Packages | bidamas, each a namespace; a `Bluefile` that is itself a blue program, pinned by its lock; registries rendered as publish workflows | [Authoring](bidamas/AUTHORING.md), [Registry](docs/REGISTRY.md) |
| Shipping | a Bluefile `app`, `image` (built by nix, distroless by default), `workload` and `service` (Kubernetes objects and a Helm chart, committed and gated fresh for GitOps), and `blue diff`, read-only | [the build stack](docs/BUILD-STACK.md) |
| Services | configuration (`settei`), entries each off or refused alone (`kousei`), postures (`shisei`), request defence (`bougyo`), retries (`saishikou`); HTTP, NATS, PostgreSQL, Valkey and JetStream; HTTP/2 framing and HPACK in pure blue | [Service architecture](docs/SERVICE-ARCHITECTURE.md), [HTTP/2](docs/HTTP2.md) |
| Documentation | this README, `AGENTS.md`, `llms.txt` and the book, rendered from one source per fact, every example run | [Documentation](docs/DOCUMENTATION.md), [Markdown](docs/MARKDOWN.md) |
| Editors | a tree-sitter grammar generated from blue's own grammar spec | [tree-sitter](docs/NATURALIZE-TREESITTER.md) |
| WebAssembly | the whole pipeline compiled to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with no host imports at all | [`blue-lang-wasm`](crates/blue-lang-wasm) |

## Commands

Every command `blue` takes, read from its own argument parser when this file
was rendered. `blue help COMMAND` shows each one's flags.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `blue FILE [ARGS]...` | Run a program as a script: quiet, and every argument after the file reaches `argv`. |
| `blue run FILE [ARGS]...` | Parse, type-check, erase, and execute a program. |
| `blue fmt FILE...` | Format a program. |
| `blue ast FILE` | Print the tatara-lisp form, annotations intact. |
| `blue erase FILE` | Print the tatara-lisp form after type erasure — what actually runs. |
| `blue check [FILE]` | Check a program against every rule in the registry — unbound names, unused bindings, types, waivers — and report the typing analysis. |
| `blue query QUERY [PATHS]...` | Every definition under PATH (files, or directories of `.b` files; `.` when none) that satisfies QUERY, one line per hit: `file:line:col: definition  name = value…`. |
| `blue migrate FILES...` | Make every reference each FILE makes to another bidama's definition explicit (`use("retsu", [:first])`, and the bidama's `needs`), keeping a file only when its resolved tree is proven unchanged. |
| `blue doc [NAME]` | What NAME is: its signature, doc line, namespace, tier and an example, for a builtin, `pkg::name`, or a bare name across the builtins and every bidama on BLUE_PATH; a bidama's name lists the package. |
| `blue verbs ARGS...` | The verb graph (`bidamas/mokuroku/graph`): `import` region or merged TSVs into its row files, `export` them back to TSV (the only writer of TSV), `check` its gates against the recorded baseline, `findings` of a TSV directory. |
| `blue explain-name NAME AT` | How a bare NAME resolves at FILE:LINE: every tier of the resolution order, what each holds, and which wins. |
| `blue census [ROOT]` | Count, over every `.b` file under ROOT, each finding of every rule still being ratcheted in, and fail unless each count equals its registry row's `ratchet`. |
| `blue explain [CODE]` | Explain a diagnostic code (`blue explain B0001`), or list them all. |
| `blue test FILE` | Check the file (as `blue check` does), then run its `test` blocks. |
| `blue profile FILE [ARGS]...` | Run a program and report every function it called: calls, inclusive and exclusive time, and what it allocated, most exclusive time first. |
| `blue trace DEF FILE [ARGS]...` | Run a program and print each call of DEF with its arguments, and each exit with its value, to stderr. |
| `blue deps FILE` | Resolve a Bluefile's dependencies. |
| `blue posture FILE` | Report the posture a Bluefile's declared floor requires. |
| `blue bluefile FILES...` | Print a Bluefile's evaluated manifest, or confirm its lock is fresh. |
| `blue lock [DIRS]...` | Evaluate each directory's Bluefile, pin every `source(...)` with `nix flake prefetch`, and write `Bluefile.lock` beside it. |
| `blue bundle FILE` | Seal FILE into an appliance payload: the program compiled (every `use` resolved, checked, erased) with the capability record its project's fresh `Bluefile.lock` verified, closed with its BLAKE3 digest. |
| `blue lsp` | Run the language server, speaking LSP over stdin/stdout. |
| `blue serve` | Serve one evaluation session as JSON lines on stdin/stdout (`theory/BLUE-TOOLING.md` §4): the door an editor drives. |
| `blue repl` | An evaluation session at the terminal. |
| `blue eval TARGET` | Evaluate EXPR, or the top-level form at FILE:LINE:COL in that file's context, and print its value. |
| `blue banner` | Print blue's wordmark. |
| `blue shift FILE` | Report the blueshift: how far this program is shifted, and what is shifting it. |
| `blue morph` | The morphology: what each posture grants, what it forfeits, which pairs are genuinely exclusive, and which language each shape corresponds to. |
| `blue reference` | Print the language reference as JSON: operators, keywords, surface forms, Bluefile words, every bound name and every command, each read from the table the implementation runs on. |
| `blue replay TRACE` | Run a crashed process again from the trace its crash wrote, and say whether it crashed the same way. |
| `blue crash dump CRASH` | What a crash violated and where: its class, the host name and capability a breach demanded, the breaching call's file, line and column, the hold, the exit and the mailbox. |
| `blue crash bisect CRASH` | The fewest messages the process took that still replay to the same crash, found by delta debugging against deterministic replay; the reduced trace is written beside the original under its own hash. |
| `blue crash immunize CRASH` | The crash's regression lock: a test that spawns the target, sends it the fewest messages that crashed it and asserts it took them, red until the target is fixed. |
| `blue arika like [FILE[:LINE]]` | The words a draft already is: each definition of FILE (or the one at FILE:LINE) matched to a blue word by def hash (T0), written shape (T1) and shape through a wrapper (T2), with the word's id and import line. |
| `blue arika word NAME` | Find a blue word by NAME: its canonical spelling, an old spelling's new home, and catalogue glosses that mention NAME (T5). |
| `blue receipt verify FILE` | Recompute a receipt's name from its bytes and check its form; any edit fails. |
| `blue config [TIER]` | Show the bounds `blue` is running with, at any tier. |
| `blue new NAME` | Start a program (a project with its own bidama), a `--bidama`, a `--script`, or a `--kernel` program, each passing `blue test` as written. |
| `blue watch [CMD] PATH... [-- ARGS]...` | Rerun `check` (the default), `test` or `run` over each PATH whenever a watched file changes: `blue watch test lib.b`. |
| `blue image build [NAME] [-- NIX_ARGS]...` | Build an `image(...)` through nix and report the tarball, its size and its layers. |
| `blue workload render [NAME]` | Print a workload's rendered objects, or with `--write` rewrite every workload's committed `output` file. |
| `blue diff [NAME]` | Compare the committed workload files with a cluster, read-only: exit 0 when they agree, 1 when they differ, 2 when the comparison failed. |
| `blue registry render [BACKEND]` | Print one backend's workflow, or with --write rewrite every standing backend's committed output. |
| `blue registry status` | The sui state of every pin: warm on the origin SUI_CACHE_URL names, cold, or absent; never fails. |

## The language in numbers

Counted from the tables the implementation runs on, when this file was
rendered:

| | |
|---|---|
| Built-in names | 373: 346 functions, 14 special forms, 13 macros |
| Surface forms | 32, with 13 operators and 25 reserved words |
| Check rules | 76: 42 fix themselves, 8 suggest a fix |
| Bluefile words | 26 |
| Commands | 44 |

## The standard library

<details>
<summary>Every bidama, with the purpose its <code>@moduledoc</code> states</summary>

65 packages, 5708 definitions, 1900 tests.

- [angou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#angou) (暗号) — number theory and the classical ciphers built on it.
- [baito](bidamas/CATALOG.md#baito) (バイト) — bytes as data: integers at a declared width and order, and record layouts that say where each field sits.
- [bunsho](bidamas/CATALOG.md#bunsho) (文書) — Markdown as a first-class value: `.md` text parsed into one typed tree whose node kinds are the ones CommonMark, GitHub Flavored Markdown and mdast agree on, the tree rendered back in one canonical formatting, and the tree read by node, by kind and by section.
- [burauza](bidamas/CATALOG.md#burauza) (ブラウザ) — the browser: what a blue page needs from the browser, generated.
- [chokkan](bidamas/CATALOG.md#chokkan) (直感) — System One judgment: typed questions in, calibrated answers out.
- [chozou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#chozou) (貯蔵, storage) — what a service keeps and reads back.
- [deeta](bidamas/CATALOG.md#deeta) (データ) — JSON data, read safely.
- [eigyou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#eigyou) (営業, open for business) — what a running service answers, guards and reports.
- [fairu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#fairu) (ファイル) — files: paths and the files they name.
- [fuuin](bidamas/CATALOG.md#fuuin) (封印) — k-of-n threshold signing: a group whose key no one share holds, signed by any k of its n shares in two rounds, RFC 9591 FROST over Ed25519.
- [gamen](bidamas/CATALOG.md#gamen) (画面) — screen: what a program shows, as values: colors and themes, UI trees rendered to HTML, and styled text, tables and trees on the terminal.
- [gitto](bidamas/CATALOG.md#gitto) (ギット) — git, as verbs: a repository read as commits, refs, branches and files, and written by commit, fetch, merge, push and clone.
- [gurafu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#gurafu) (グラフ) — directed graphs as values: build them, ask them, order them.
- [hadome](bidamas/CATALOG.md#hadome) (歯止め) — a baseline ratchet: recorded debt may shrink or hold, never grow.
- [happa](bidamas/CATALOG.md#happa) (葉っぱ) — a template's leaves: their declaration, split, graph, change, schedule and verdicts, as pure decisions.
- [heni](bidamas/CATALOG.md#heni) (変異) — mutation testing for a blue package: each mutation changes one literal in a fresh copy of the package, runs its tests, and must make them fail.
- [hikisuu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#hikisuu) (引数) — command-line arguments: one declared spec is parsed into a record, rendered as help, and answered as shell completion.
- [hizuke](bidamas/CATALOG.md#hizuke) (日付) — the proleptic Gregorian calendar, as arithmetic.
- [hon](bidamas/CATALOG.md#hon) (本) — a project's book: its pages, each of one Diátaxis kind, rendered into the files a reader or an agent opens.
- [ibuki](bidamas/CATALOG.md#ibuki) (息吹) — the plane an app docks into, as pure decisions: the five structural classes and a docking check over the reach `blue lock` measured, the Flash channel's token bucket, the Tide channel's LEDBAT controller, and a Strand, a last-writer-wins map whose every transition is a hash-linked record of its input and output roots.
- [isshou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#isshou) (一生, a lifetime) — what a thing goes through, recorded and read back.
- [jisho](bidamas/CATALOG.md#jisho) (辞書) — dictionaries: maps as values, read and changed by key, each change a new map.
- [junjo](bidamas/CATALOG.md#junjo) (順序) — ordering: sorting, searching, selection.
- [kaaneru](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kaaneru) (カーネル) — the Linux kernel, spoken from blue: maps, programs, links and ring buffers over `bpf(2)`, with every struct a `baito` layout and no C library in the path.
- [kakehashi](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kakehashi) (架け橋, a bridge) — blue speaks Nix, Nix runs blue, and a rebuild does
- [kansuu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kansuu) (関数) — functions about functions.
- [kazu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kazu) (数) — numbers.
- [keiyu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#keiyu) (経由) — by way of: run one command with a proxy set for it alone.
- [khipu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#khipu) — blue's knowledge graph (docs/KHIPU.md): RDF terms as a closed sum, quads, and N-Triples and N-Quads read and written. A literal with both a language tag and a datatype has no constructor, an IRI or a language tag that is not valid is refused where it is read, and a blank node carries the scope of the document it came from, so two documents' `_:b` are two nodes.
- [kiwari](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kiwari) (木割): one grammar spec, every syntax artifact emitted from it.
- [kodou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kodou) (鼓動) — the dual-pulse wire: a Flash channel paced by ibuki's token bucket and a Tide channel paced by ibuki's LEDBAT controller from the one-way delay each acknowledgement measures, over one UDP socket the host frames (0x02 Flash, 0x01 Tide); and the gossip of crash proofs on it: an alert on Flash, the artifact on Tide when a peer asks for it, verified by its content hash and kept in kensa's `kensa-immunity.v1` file.
- [koubou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#koubou) (工房, workshop) — shapes made, measured and cut.
- [kousei](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kousei) (構成) — a system composed entry by entry: each entry checked, configured off, tuned or refused alone, then judged into what stands.
- [koutei](bidamas/CATALOG.md#koutei) (工程) — one step of a pipeline, as GitHub Actions runs it.
- [kueri](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kueri) (クエリ) — queries: analysis is authored in blue, and SQL is only the rendered bridge to DuckDB.
- [kyohi](bidamas/CATALOG.md#kyohi) (拒否) — refusals, as data.
- [maakuappu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#maakuappu) (マークアップ) — XML as data: a document parsed by the runtime's xml_parse (quick-xml) into element maps {name, attributes, children, text}, the queries a reader of a scanner export asks of it (children and descendants by name, attributes, text, a path of element names), and the element rendered back with every value escaped. A DTD entity is never expanded or fetched: the document is refused (:xml_refused), and a document that is not well-formed raises :xml_malformed.
- [mitoshi](bidamas/CATALOG.md#mitoshi) (見通し, a clear view ahead) — what a running program shows of itself.
- [moji](bidamas/CATALOG.md#moji) (文字) — strings.
- [mokuroku](bidamas/CATALOG.md#mokuroku) (目録): the catalogue of what every bidama on a BLUE_PATH provides.
- [okite](bidamas/CATALOG.md#okite) (掟) — blue's decisions, each enforced by laws written in blue.
- [ongaku](bidamas/CATALOG.md#ongaku) (音楽) — twelve-tone music theory, as arithmetic on semitones.
- [ran](bidamas/CATALOG.md#ran) (乱) — deterministic pseudo-randomness.
- [retsu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#retsu) (列) — lists, made TOTAL.
- [ronri](bidamas/CATALOG.md#ronri) (論理) — predicates, and the algebra over them.
- [sabi](bidamas/CATALOG.md#sabi) (錆): Rust source from blue data. Build the items as values, render once.
- [saishikou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#saishikou) (再試行) — retrying a step that can fail for a moment.
- [seimei](bidamas/CATALOG.md#seimei) (生命) — cellular automata: elementary rules, and Life.
- [settei](bidamas/CATALOG.md#settei) (設定) — configuration, blue's shikumi: a record of defaults grouped by concern, resolved by read(app, defaults) from the defaults, then ~/.config/<app>/<app>.yaml (or <APP>_CONFIG), then <APP>_<GROUP>__<KEY> in the environment, each value typed by its default and a wrong type refused. The resolved record is read by dotted path; a misspelt path raises and names the fields that exist.
- [shinchoku](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shinchoku) (進捗) — progress: operational probes that judge by progress over a window, never by one reading.
- [shinsatsu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shinsatsu) (診察) — the credential doctor: a provider, the failure classes its credential helper can show, and for each class a diagnosis, the remediation steps and a verify step. A new provider or a new failure class is a declaration.
- [shinsuu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shinsuu) (進数) — base conversion and checksums.
- [shisutemu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shisutemu) (システム) — the system.
- [shomei](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shomei) (署名) — signatures and hash chains: Ed25519 and BLAKE3, for real.
- [shuugou](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shuugou) (集合) — sets, over plain lists.
- [shuusei](bidamas/CATALOG.md#shuusei) (修正) — amending declared data: put a value at a path, delete it, merge into it, upsert a list element, and amend a keyed set of objects by judged patch entries.
- [suugaku](bidamas/CATALOG.md#suugaku) (数学, mathematics) — numbers worked over as a discipline.
- [tesuto](bidamas/CATALOG.md#tesuto) (テスト) — testing: errors and snapshots as assertions, and the policy that holds every definition to a test beside it.
- [todokede](bidamas/CATALOG.md#todokede) (届出, filings) — what a person or a company declares as entries.
- [toriyose](bidamas/CATALOG.md#toriyose) (取り寄せ, fetching on order) — what a frontend asks for and keeps.
- [touroku](bidamas/CATALOG.md#touroku) (登録) — registry: a project published to and resolved from registry backends, each a rendering of the Bluefile, never its truth.
- [ugoki](bidamas/CATALOG.md#ugoki) (動き) — motion: how a value moves over time.
- [ukai](bidamas/CATALOG.md#ukai) (迂回) — a detour: keep an overlay VPN reaching its control plane and relays while a full-tunnel corporate VPN owns the default route.
- [utsushi](bidamas/CATALOG.md#utsushi) (写し, a transcription) — a part of a repository's history, shown as a history of its own: a lens picks the part, and each commit is written again over the part's tree, with its author, committer and message unchanged, so the same lens over the same commit gives the same commit id on every machine (docs/UTSUSHI.md).
- [zenbu](bidamas/CATALOG.md#zenbu) (全部) — the whole distribution, as ONE dependency.

</details>

## What is not built

blue states its gaps plainly, because a language's honest gaps matter more
than its claims. This list is the one in
[Implementing blue](docs/implementing.md#what-is-not-built), rendered here:

Stated so nobody cites it as existing: **no per-process GC heap** (processes have
private environments and messages are deep-copied, but reclamation is `Arc`
refcounting — no independent collection pause), **no registry client** (resolution
is real; nothing fetches), **no self-hosting on the implementation axis**
(`spec/*.b` is the specification axis only), **no comment attachment inside a
form**, **no entropy primitive and no encryption** (the `crypto` layer hashes,
signs and verifies; a keypair comes from a seed the caller supplies),
**no TLS** (`net` speaks NATS and HTTP over plain TCP: an `https://` url and a
NATS server requiring TLS are refused by name; planned in `docs/HTTP2.md` P4,
rustls with ALPN `h2`),
**no import EMISSION into a wasm module** (`blue_lang_waku::imports_of`
derives the table from a frame — nothing puts an entry into a `.wasm`, and no
engine border is wired: that is `BLUE-EXECUTION.md` M2, blocked on `tatara-wasm`
not being on crates.io), **no editor answer inside a broken buffer** (the
LSP answers from the newest revision that parsed until the parser recovers,
`BLUE-ENGINE.md` E6), **project rules in the editor or as wasm** (`blue check`
runs them in-process under the rule frame; the LSP does not run them, and the
ABI is shaped for a wasm module that nothing builds yet), **no account of a
move the send ring cannot carry** (from a held node a moved plain process
brings its tape, mailbox journal and host-call count, `blue-image` version 5,
and a moved server its journal, count and the root of the state its
incarnation began with, version 6, so each crash trace and receipt covers the
whole incarnation; an account past the tape bound or the send ring stays
behind, and that process's journal, count and a server's receipt
`input_root` start at the node it moved to), **no link across nodes** (`evict` breaks a link and
tells a partner that traps exits; it refuses one that does not), **no
authenticated image** (an image's BLAKE3 name proves it arrived whole, not who
sent it; it runs under the accepting node's frame, never more), and no **`case`/`when` pattern matching** or **ranges** — the two remaining
surface gaps a Ruby or Elixir author would reach for. `theory/BLUE.md` §V.26 holds the tier ledger; **do not build against a
DESIGN-tier row without saying so.**

## Theming

Colours come from [irodori](https://github.com/pleme-io/irodori), the fleet's
Nord palette. blue carries no hex of its own. `nord10` (`#5E81AC`, deep frost
blue) is its identity, and `nord8` frost cyan stays the fleet's shared
interaction colour: identity and interaction are different roles. The mark is
a blueshift too: four solid cells walk Nord's Frost band toward blue. It names
each colour by ANSI slot, never by hex, so it renders in your Nord and follows
you when you retheme.

## Building blue

```console host
$ nix build .#blue
$ nix flake check
$ cargo test --workspace
```

`nix build` is hermetic. `nix flake check` runs every gate the root
`Bluefile` declares. This README is rendered by `hon` from
[`docs/introduction.md`](docs/introduction.md), the first tutorial, the
implementation's own tables and the catalogue; edit those, then run
`nix run .#regen`. Changing blue itself starts at [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

MIT.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/install.md`

# Install blue

You need [Nix](https://nixos.org) with flakes turned on. Install blue into
your profile:

```console host
$ nix profile install github:pleme-io/blue
```

To try blue without installing it, put `nix run github:pleme-io/blue --` in
front of each command below.

Ask blue for a value:

```console
$ blue eval '1 + 2'
3
```

Write a file called `hello.b`:

```blue file=hello.b
write_stdout(unlines(["Olá, mundo!"]))
```

Run it:

```console
$ blue hello.b
Olá, mundo!
```

That is a whole blue program. The next tutorial, [a first script](docs/tutorial/first-script.md),
gives it arguments.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-script.md`

# A first script

A script is one file that runs from the command line. It needs no project
and no configuration.

Write `greet.b`:

```blue file=greet.b
#!/usr/bin/env blue
def greeting(who)
  "hello, #{who}"
end

write_stdout(unlines([greeting(argv_get(0, "world"))]))
```

`argv_get(0, "world")` reads the first argument, or `"world"` when there is
none. Run the script with and without one:

```console
$ blue greet.b
hello, world
$ blue greet.b ryn
hello, ryn
```

The first line is a shebang. After `chmod +x greet.b`, the script also runs as
`./greet.b ryn`.

blue writes one formatting. Ask it whether the file is in that form:

```console
$ blue fmt --check greet.b
```

No output means yes. `blue fmt --write` puts a file into the form.

`blue new --script` starts a script for you, already executable and already
formatted:

```console
$ blue new --script tool.b
created tool.b, executable
run it   ./tool.b  (or blue tool.b)
$ blue tool.b a b
hello, a (2 argument(s))
```

A script can `use` every standard bidama with no setup. When a script
outgrows one file, it becomes [a first program](docs/tutorial/first-program.md).

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-program.md`

# A first program

A program is a project: a `Bluefile` that says how it is built, a `main.b`
that runs it, and its code in a bidama of its own. `blue new` writes one that
passes its tests as written:

```console
$ blue new tally
created tally/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, flake.nix, main.b, bidamas/tally/
run it   blue tally/main.b
test it  blue test tally/bidamas/tally/tally.b
$ cd tally
$ blue main.b ryn
hello, ryn
```

Now make it count words. Replace `bidamas/tally/tally.b` with this:

```blue file=bidamas/tally/tally.b
use("retsu", [:size])

def words(text)
  filter((w) -> w != "", split(text, " "))
end

def tally(text)
  size(words(text))
end

def main(args)
  write_stdout(unlines([to_s(tally(join(args, " ")))]))
end

test "words are what the spaces separate"
  assert tally("one two  three") == 3
end

test "an empty text has no words"
  assert tally("") == 0
end
```

Run the tests. `blue test` checks the file first, then runs each `test`
block:

```console
$ blue test bidamas/tally/tally.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

Run the program:

```console
$ blue main.b the quick brown fox
4
```

`main.b` stayed the same: it calls `main(argv)` from the `tally` bidama. Next,
[a first bidama](docs/tutorial/first-bidama.md) documents a package so others can use it.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-bidama.md`

# A first bidama

A bidama is a blue package. It documents itself: a `@moduledoc` says what
the package is for, and a `@doc` above each definition says what it does,
with an example that `blue test` runs.

Start a program, then a second bidama beside its own:

```console
$ blue new shelf
created shelf/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, flake.nix, main.b, bidamas/shelf/
run it   blue shelf/main.b
test it  blue test shelf/bidamas/shelf/shelf.b
$ cd shelf/bidamas
$ blue new --bidama prose
created prose/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, prose.b
test it  blue test prose/prose.b
$ cd ..
```

Replace `bidamas/prose/prose.b` with a documented package:

```blue file=bidamas/prose/prose.b
@moduledoc """
prose: split text into words and count them.

    count_words("a b") #=> 2
"""

use("retsu", [:size])

@doc """
words: The words of a text: the runs of characters between spaces.

    words(" a  b ") #=> ["a", "b"]
"""
def words(text)
  filter((w) -> w != "", split(text, " "))
end

@doc """
count_words: How many words a text holds.

    count_words("the quick brown fox") #=> 4
"""
def count_words(text)
  size(words(text))
end

test "an empty text has no words"
  assert count_words("") == 0
end
```

Each `expr #=> value` line in a doc is a doctest. `blue test` runs them with
the `test` blocks:

```console
$ blue test bidamas/prose/prose.b
4 test(s): 4 passed, 0 failed
```

`blue doc` shows a definition as a reader sees it:

```console
$ BLUE_PATH=bidamas blue doc prose::count_words
prose::count_words(text)
  bidama prose · tier: qualified
  count_words: How many words a text holds.
  
      count_words("the quick brown fox") #=> 4
  · signature `def count_words(text)` · rung dynamic
  · pure: reaches no host capability
  example (test "an empty text has no words"):
    assert count_words("") == 0
```

Now use the package from the program. Replace `bidamas/shelf/shelf.b`:

```blue file=bidamas/shelf/shelf.b
use("prose", [:count_words])

def main(args)
  write_stdout(unlines(["#{count_words(join(args, " "))} words"]))
end

test "the program counts its arguments' words"
  assert count_words("a b c") == 3
end
```

A bidama's `Bluefile` and lock record the packages its files use. `shelf`
now uses `prose` and no longer uses `retsu`, so the check refuses the old
lock and names its fixer. Run it, then run the program:

```console
$ blue check --fix bidamas/shelf/shelf.b
$ blue main.b one two three
3 words
```

The next tutorial, [a first service](docs/tutorial/first-service.md), declares a service
in the `Bluefile`.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-service.md`

# A first service

A service is one declaration and one program. The declaration names what the
service needs; blue renders the chart, the settings schema, the image and
the checks from it. This tutorial builds a small copy of
[ola-mundo](https://github.com/pleme-io/ola-mundo), the reference blue service.

Make a directory for the service, and declare it in a `Bluefile`:

```console
$ mkdir hello
$ cd hello
```

```blue file=Bluefile
package("hello", "0.1.0")

service(
  "hello",
  {
    program: "hello.b",
    repository: "ghcr.io/example/hello",
    port: 8080,
    config: {greeting: "Olá", subject: "mundo"}
  }
)

check("hello", "hello.b")
```

The program answers `GET /`. `settei` reads the settings the declaration
gives it, and `kyuuji` serves HTTP:

```blue file=hello.b
use("kyuuji")
use("settei")

def greeting(s, who)
  subject = if who == nil or who == ""
    settei::setting(s, "subject")
  else
    who
  end
  "#{settei::setting(s, "greeting")}, #{subject}!"
end

def handle(s, req)
  if get(req, :method) == "GET" and get(req, :path) == "/"
    kyuuji::text(200, unlines([greeting(s, kyuuji::query_param(req, "who"))]))
  else
    kyuuji::not_found(req)
  end
end

if settei::serving?
  s = settei::current
  kyuuji::serve_settings(s, (req) -> handle(s, req))
end

def settings()
  {"greeting" => "Olá", "subject" => "mundo"}
end

test "the root greets the configured subject"
  r = handle(settings, kyuuji::request("GET", "/", ""))
  assert get(r, :status) == 200
  assert get(r, :body) == unlines(["Olá, mundo!"])
end

test "any other path is not found"
  assert get(handle(settings, kyuuji::request("GET", "/x", "")), :status) ==
    404
end
```

The handler is a function from a request to a response, so the tests call
it directly. Lock the declaration and run the tests:

```console
$ blue lock .
./Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
$ blue test hello.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

The `haibi` bidama renders the declaration into everything that ships the
service. This program lists the files it would write:

```blue file=../show.b
use("haibi", [:files])
use("retsu", [:first])

m = get(json_read(read_file("hello/Bluefile.lock")), "manifest")
spec = get(get(m, "services"), "hello")
paths = map(first, files("hello", get(m, "version"), spec))
write_stdout(unlines(sort_keyed((p) -> p, paths)))
```

```console
$ cd ..
$ blue show.b
chart/Chart.yaml
chart/files/dashboard.json
chart/templates/NOTES.txt
chart/templates/dashboard.yaml
chart/templates/deployment.yaml
chart/templates/service.yaml
chart/templates/serviceaccount.yaml
chart/templates/slo-rules.yaml
chart/values.schema.json
chart/values.yaml
config/hello.schema.json
config/hello.yaml
```

A real service adds a one-line `flake.nix` (`blue.lib.project { src = ./.; }`,
as ola-mundo has). Then nix builds the image and runs every check:

```console host
$ nix flake check
```

The [how-to guides](docs/howto/test-and-doctest.md) each do one task from
here.

---

Source: `docs/tutorial/first-kernel-program.md`

# A first kernel program

A kernel program is a function in blue. Blue compiles it to BPF. The same source
then runs in two places: a pure machine that needs no kernel, and a real Linux
kernel. This tutorial writes a program that counts packets by protocol and drops
ICMP. You need no root and no Linux until the last section.

`blue new --kernel` starts a project that passes its tests as written:

```console
$ blue new --kernel pkts
created pkts/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, flake.nix, pkts.b
test it  cd pkts && blue test pkts.b
run it   cd pkts && sudo blue run --allow host --quiet pkts.b -- eth0
$ cd pkts
$ blue test --filter "on the machine" pkts.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

The `--filter` keeps the two tests that run on the machine. The file holds one
more test, and that test needs a kernel. Without `--filter`, a host with no kernel
says which test it skipped and why, and the tally counts it apart from a pass:

```console host
$ blue test pkts.b
SKIP on a real kernel, the program counts what the machine counts: no kernel here: this host is not Linux
3 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped
```

Now make the program drop ICMP. Replace `pkts.b` with this:

```blue file=pkts.b
use(
  "bpf",
  %i[compile declare_map map_add packet_int packet_len xdp_drop xdp_pass]
)

use("kaaneru", %i[attached install kernel_absence])
use("retsu", %i[first repeat])
use("tesuto", [:skip_for])

COUNTS = declare_map(:counts, :array, 4, 8, 256)

ICMP = 1

def filter_packets(ctx)
  if packet_len(ctx) < 34
    xdp_pass
  else
    protocol = packet_int(ctx, 23, 1)
    map_add(COUNTS, protocol, 1)
    if protocol == ICMP
      xdp_drop
    else
      xdp_pass
    end
  end
end

def program()
  compile("pkts.b", {entry: :filter_packets, kind: :xdp, on_fault: xdp_pass})
end

def frame(protocol)
  append(*[repeat(0, 23), [protocol], repeat(0, 10)])
end

def main()
  index = to_int(trim(read_file("/sys/class/net/#{first(argv)}/ifindex")))
  attached(
    program,
    {xdp: index},
    fn(live)
      sleep_ms(5000)
      dropped = kaaneru::map_int(live, :counts, ICMP)
      write_stdout(unlines(["ICMP packets dropped: #{to_s(dropped)}"]))
    end
  )
end

test "on the machine, ICMP is counted and dropped"
  p = program
  st = bpf::run(p, {packet: frame(ICMP), maps: p[:maps]})
  assert st.ret == xdp_drop
  assert bpf::map_int(st, :counts, ICMP) == 1
end

test "on the machine, TCP is counted and passed"
  p = program
  st = bpf::run(p, {packet: frame(6), maps: p[:maps]})
  assert st.ret == xdp_pass
  assert bpf::map_int(st, :counts, 6) == 1
  assert bpf::map_int(st, :counts, ICMP) == 0
end

test "on the machine, a frame too short for the field is passed and not counted"
  p = program
  st = bpf::run(p, {packet: repeat(0, 20), maps: p[:maps]})
  assert st.ret == xdp_pass
  assert bpf::map_int(st, :counts, 0) == 0
end

test "on a real kernel, the program decides as the machine decides"
  skip_for(kernel_absence)
  live = install(program)
  assert kaaneru::run(live[:prog], {packet: frame(ICMP)})[:ret] == xdp_drop
  assert kaaneru::run(live[:prog], {packet: frame(6)})[:ret] == xdp_pass
  assert kaaneru::map_int(live, :counts, ICMP) == 1
end
```

Each part has one job:

- `declare_map` states a map's shape: the machine and the kernel read the same
  shape.
- `filter_packets` is the kernel program. It runs only when compiled, and the
  compiler writes the bounds check each packet read needs.
- `compile` turns it into BPF and checks it first. `on_fault` is what the program
  answers when a read falls outside the packet.
- `bpf::run` runs the program on the pure machine. `bpf::map_int` reads a map on
  it.
- `attached` loads the program onto one hook, runs a function, and takes the
  program away whatever the function does.
- `kaaneru::map_int` reads a map in the kernel, with the same arguments.

Run the tests:

```console
$ blue test --filter "on the machine" pkts.b
3 test(s): 3 passed, 0 failed
```

A program the kernel cannot take stops before it reaches the kernel. Blue
fractions have no BPF form, so this program never compiles:

```blue file=../fraction.b
use("bpf", [:compile])

def half(_ctx)
  7 / 2
end

compile("fraction.b", {entry: :half, kind: :xdp, on_fault: 0})
```

```console
$ cd ..
```

```console fails
$ blue fraction.b
bpf_compile
fraction
```

## On a real kernel

This section needs Linux and root. The test that needs a kernel runs the program
through `BPF_PROG_RUN`, which attaches nothing:

```console host
$ cd pkts
$ sudo blue test pkts.b
4 test(s): 4 passed, 0 failed
```

To see real packets, make a network namespace, so nothing on your host sees the
hook. Run the loader in one terminal:

```console host
$ sudo ip netns add demo
$ sudo ip netns exec demo ip link set lo up
$ sudo ip netns exec demo blue run --allow host --quiet pkts.b -- lo
ICMP packets dropped: 3
```

While the loader waits five seconds, ping from a second terminal. The pings get
no answer, and when the loader ends the program is gone:

```console host
$ sudo ip netns exec demo ping -c 3 -W 1 127.0.0.1
$ sudo ip netns del demo
```

Next: [pick a hook](docs/howto/pick-a-kernel-hook.md),
[read a kernel field](docs/howto/read-a-kernel-field.md),
[debug a refusal](docs/howto/debug-a-kernel-refusal.md) and
[ship a node agent](docs/howto/ship-a-node-agent.md). The words and what each has
been measured on are in [KERNEL.md](docs/KERNEL.md).

---

Source: `docs/howto/test-and-doctest.md`

# Write a test and a doctest

Put a `test` block beside the code it tests, in the same file. `assert`
fails the test when its expression is false:

```blue file=math.b
@doc """
double: Twice a number.

    double(21) #=> 42
"""
def double(n)
  n * 2
end

test "double of zero is zero"
  assert double(0) == 0
end

test "double of a negative stays negative"
  assert double(-3) == -6
end
```

The `#=>` line in the `@doc` is a doctest: `blue test` runs it beside the
`test` blocks.

```console
$ blue test math.b
3 test(s): 3 passed, 0 failed
```

Run only the tests whose name holds a word:

```console
$ blue test --filter negative math.b
1 test(s): 1 passed, 0 failed
```

A failure prints the expression as you wrote it, with both sides:

```blue file=wrong.b
test "two and two"
  assert 2 + 2 == 5
end
```

```console fails
$ blue test wrong.b
FAIL two and two
  assert 2 + 2 == 5
```

A test that cannot run on this host says why, and the tally counts it apart from
a pass. Here the reason is always there; `kaaneru::kernel_absence` gives a real one:

```blue file=needs.b
use("tesuto", [:skip_for])

def why_not()
  "this host has no such device"
end

test "it needs a device"
  skip_for(why_not)
  assert false
end

test "it needs nothing"
  assert true
end
```

```console
$ blue test needs.b
2 test(s): 1 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped
```

On a host where every test must run, make each skip a failure:

```console fails
$ BLUE_TEST_SKIP=refuse blue test needs.b
skipped under BLUE_TEST_SKIP=refuse: this host has no such device
```

`blue test DIR` runs every file under a directory that holds a test, in
parallel.

---

Source: `docs/howto/climb-the-blueshift.md`

# Climb the blueshift

`blue shift` names the rung a file stands on: dynamic, annotated, checked or
restricted. You climb by annotating definitions.

Start with a file that declares nothing:

```blue file=area.b
def area(w, h)
  w * h
end

def square(s)
  area(s, s)
end
```

```console
$ blue shift area.b
█░░░ dynamic  (0/2 typed, 0 nodes analysed)
no annotations — no analysis runs, and nothing is checked

  · untyped declaration      `area` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
  · untyped declaration      `square` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
```

Annotate `area`. The file moves up one rung, and `blue shift` names what
still holds it back:

```blue file=area.b
def area(w: Int, h: Int) -> Int
  w * h
end

def square(s)
  area(s, s)
end
```

```console
$ blue shift area.b
██░░ annotated  (1/2 typed, 3 nodes analysed)
some declarations are typed; untyped ones are unchecked

  → type annotation          `area` is annotated, so it is checked
  · untyped declaration      `square` has no annotation — annotate it to shift further
```

Annotate `square` too, and every declaration is checked:

```blue file=area.b
def area(w: Int, h: Int) -> Int
  w * h
end

def square(s: Int) -> Int
  area(s, s)
end
```

```console
$ blue shift area.b
███░ checked  (2/2 typed, 6 nodes analysed)
every declaration is typed, so the whole file is checked

  → type annotation          `area` is annotated, so it is checked
  → type annotation          `square` is annotated, so it is checked
```

A wrong annotation is now an error before the program runs:

```blue file=bad.b
def half(n: Int) -> Int
  "half"
end
```

```console fails
$ blue check bad.b
error[B0003]: `half` declares it returns Int, but its body produces Str
```

The `pleme-io/actions/blue-shift` action holds a project to a floor rung in
CI.

---

Source: `docs/howto/declare-access.md`

# Declare what a program may touch

A program that runs with no flag may reach every host capability. `--allow`
holds a run to the ones you name: `none`, `host`, or any of `process`,
`filesystem`, `environment`, `clock`, `network` and `entropy`.

Here is a program that reads a file:

```blue file=peek.b
write_stdout(read_file("note.txt"))
```

```blue file=note.txt
a note
```

With `--allow none`, blue refuses it before it runs, and names the flag that
grants it:

```console fails
$ blue run --allow none --quiet peek.b
refused: `read_file` reaches the host (filesystem)
```

Grant exactly what it needs:

```console
$ blue run --allow filesystem --quiet peek.b
a note
```

A script states its capabilities in its shebang, so `./peek.b` carries them
with it:

```blue file=peek2.b
#!/usr/bin/env -S blue --allow filesystem
write_stdout(read_file("note.txt"))
```

Every Rust guarantee, the blue gate that matches it and its off switch are in
[SAFETY.md](docs/SAFETY.md). One access declaration for a whole service, in its
`service(...)` entry, is designed in
[SERVICE-ACCESS.md](docs/SERVICE-ACCESS.md) and not built yet.

---

Source: `docs/howto/write-an-action.md`

# Write an action

A pleme-io action keeps its logic in a `run.b`. The `koutei` bidama is that
file's side of the step: it reads the `INPUT_*` variables, writes outputs and
the step summary, and fails the step.

Write `run.b`:

```blue file=run.b
use("koutei", [:fail, :input_or, :output])

who = input_or("who", "world")
if who == "nobody"
  fail("there is nobody to greet")
end
output("greeting", "hello, #{who}")
```

Run it the way the runner does: inputs as `INPUT_*` variables, outputs to the
file `GITHUB_OUTPUT` names.

```console
$ INPUT_WHO=ryn GITHUB_OUTPUT=out.txt blue run --quiet run.b
$ cat out.txt
greeting<<KOUTEI_EOF
hello, ryn
KOUTEI_EOF
```

With no `GITHUB_OUTPUT`, `koutei` prints the record, so a local run shows it:

```console
$ blue run --quiet run.b
greeting<<KOUTEI_EOF
hello, world
KOUTEI_EOF
```

A refused input fails the step with an error annotation:

```console fails
$ INPUT_WHO=nobody blue run --quiet run.b
::error::there is nobody to greet
```

The `action.yml` beside it passes the inputs and runs the file:

```yaml
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - shell: bash
      env:
        INPUT_WHO: ${{ inputs.who }}
      run: blue run --quiet "${{ github.action_path }}/run.b"
```

`pleme-io/actions/blue-shift` is a complete example.

---

Source: `docs/howto/publish-a-bidama.md`

# Publish a bidama

A bidama is reachable when it sits under a `packages` root: a directory of
packages, each with its own `Bluefile`. A project finds packages through its
own `packages(...)` roots, then `BLUE_PATH`, then the distribution compiled
into `blue`.

Make a library of one package:

```console
$ mkdir lib
$ cd lib
$ blue new --bidama greet
created greet/: Bluefile, Bluefile.lock, greet.b
test it  blue test greet/greet.b
$ cd ..
```

Another project reaches it with `BLUE_PATH`:

```blue file=app.b
use("greet", [:greeting])

write_stdout(unlines([greeting(["ryn"])]))
```

```console
$ BLUE_PATH=lib blue app.b
hello, ryn
```

A project publishes itself with `registry(...)` entries in its `Bluefile`.
Each entry is one backend. The backend renders from the `Bluefile` and its
lock, which stay the truth. `package`'s third argument sets visibility once:

```blue file=lib/Bluefile
package("greetings", "0.1.0", :public)

packages(".")
registry(:sui, {outputs: ["default"]})
```

```console
$ cd lib
$ blue lock .
./Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
```

`blue registry render --write` then writes each backend's publish workflow.
In blue's own distribution, a new package also needs a row in
`bidamas/NAMES.md`: the build is red without one. The full design is
[REGISTRY.md](docs/REGISTRY.md).

---

Source: `docs/howto/pure-worker.md`

# Run a pure worker

A pure worker turns data into data. It reads no file, no clock and no
environment. `--allow none` holds a run to that, and blue proves it before
the program starts.

Write the transformation and its tests in one file:

```blue file=totals.b
def line_total(item)
  item.price * item.qty
end

def total(items)
  reduce((sum, item) -> sum + line_total(item), 0, items)
end

test "an empty order costs nothing"
  assert total([]) == 0
end

test "a total sums price times quantity"
  assert total([{price: 2, qty: 3}, {price: 5, qty: 1}]) == 11
end

def main()
  order = [{price: 2, qty: 3}, {price: 5, qty: 1}]
  write_stdout(unlines(["total: #{total(order)}"]))
end
```

Test it:

```console
$ blue test totals.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

Run it with no host capability:

```console
$ blue run --allow none --quiet totals.b
total: 11
```

Now add a timestamp to the output. `now_ms` reads the host clock:

```blue file=stamped.b
def total(items)
  reduce((sum, item) -> sum + item.price * item.qty, 0, items)
end

def main()
  order = [{price: 2, qty: 3}, {price: 5, qty: 1}]
  write_stdout(unlines(["#{now_ms} total: #{total(order)}"]))
end
```

The check stage refuses this variant, and no line of it runs. The message
names the call, the capability and the flag that grants it:

```console fails
$ blue run --allow none --quiet stamped.b
blue: 1 error(s) in the check stage:
stamped.b: refused: `now_ms` reaches the host (clock), which this run does not allow; pass --allow clock to grant it
```

Keep the host call out of the worker. Make the call in the code that uses the
worker, and give the worker the value. To keep `now_ms` in a program and
still get the same output at each run, give it a stepped clock:
[Virtualize a capability](docs/howto/virtualize-a-capability.md). The other capability
names are in [Declare what a program may touch](docs/howto/declare-access.md).

---

Source: `docs/howto/supervise-processes.md`

# Supervise processes

A supervisor starts child processes and restarts a child that crashes. A
child is a function that loops on `receive`. Here each child keeps a running
sum and raises on a negative number:

```blue file=tally.b
def tally(parent, sum)
  n = receive()
  if n < 0
    raise(:negative, "cannot add #{n}")
  end
  send(parent, [:sum, self, sum + n])
  tally(parent, sum + n)
end

def add(worker, n)
  send(worker, n)
  receive([:sum, worker, :_])[2]
end

def crash(worker)
  send(worker, -1)
  receive(:never, 50)
end

def after_middle_crash(strategy)
  sup = supervisor(
    strategy,
    [[tally, [self, 0]], [tally, [self, 0]], [tally, [self, 0]]],
    3
  )
  workers = children(sup)
  map((w) -> add(w, 1), workers)
  crash(workers[1])
  map((w) -> add(w, 1), workers)
end

test "one_for_one restarts only the child that crashed"
  assert after_middle_crash(:one_for_one) == [2, 1, 2]
end

test "one_for_all restarts every child"
  assert after_middle_crash(:one_for_all) == [1, 1, 1]
end

test "rest_for_one restarts the crashed child and the ones after it"
  assert after_middle_crash(:rest_for_one) == [2, 1, 1]
end

test "past max_restarts the supervisor gives up"
  sup = supervisor(:one_for_one, [[tally, [self, 0]]], 1)
  worker = first(children(sup))
  crash(worker)
  assert alive?(worker)
  crash(worker)
  assert not alive?(worker)
end

def main()
  sup = supervisor(:one_for_one, [[tally, [self, 0]]], 3)
  worker = first(children(sup))
  add(worker, 2)
  write_stdout(unlines(["before the crash: #{add(worker, 3)}"]))
  crash(worker)
  write_stdout(unlines(["after the restart: #{add(worker, 4)}"]))
end
```

`supervisor(strategy, children, max_restarts)` starts each child from a
`[function, arguments]` pair and returns the supervisor's pid. `children(sup)`
gives the child pids in order. `crash` sends a negative number, then waits
50 ms for a message that never comes. The supervisor restarts the child in
that time.

Run it:

```console
$ blue run --quiet tally.b
before the crash: 5
after the restart: 4
```

The restarted child keeps its pid, so `add(worker, 4)` reaches it. It starts
again from its arguments, `[self, 0]`, with an empty mailbox, so its sum
starts again at 0. Blue also writes each crash to stderr, with the path of a
trace. `blue replay TRACE` runs the crash again.

The strategy says which children restart:

| Strategy | Restarts |
|---|---|
| `:one_for_one` | the child that crashed |
| `:one_for_all` | every child |
| `:rest_for_one` | the child that crashed and every child declared after it |

The tests crash the middle child of three, then add 1 to each child. A 2 is
a child that kept its sum. A 1 is a child that restarted. The last argument,
`max_restarts`, is 3 when you omit it. Past it, the supervisor stops and the
child stays down. The last test shows this with a limit of 1:

```console
$ blue test tally.b
4 test(s): 4 passed, 0 failed
```

---

Source: `docs/howto/virtualize-a-capability.md`

# Virtualize a capability

The Bluefile word `virtualize` binds a host capability to a pure provider.
With `using: :deterministic_stepped`, the first `now_ms` is `at_ms`, and each
read after it adds `step_ms`. The program reads the same times at every run.

```blue file=Bluefile
package("stamps", "0.1.0")
packages("bidamas")
virtualize(:clock, {using: :deterministic_stepped, at_ms: 1000, step_ms: 5})
```

```blue file=main.b
def main()
  write_stdout(unlines(["#{now_ms}", "#{now_ms}", "#{now_ms}"]))
end
```

Lock the project, then run it. `blue lock` checks the declaration and records
the provider in `Bluefile.lock`. A Bluefile with no `source` locks offline.

```console
$ blue lock .
./Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
$ blue run --quiet main.b
1000
1005
1010
```

The provider is not the host. So the same program runs under `--allow none`:

```console
$ blue run --allow none --quiet main.b
1000
1005
1010
```

## Scope the provider to one package

`for:` gives the provider only to the packages it names, and to what they
use. The rest of the program gets the host clock, or a refusal when the
Bluefile does not `allow` it. Here `allow([])` grants nothing, and only the
`ledger` package gets the stepped clock:

```blue file=books/Bluefile
package("books", "0.1.0")
packages("bidamas")
allow([])

virtualize(
  :clock,
  {using: :deterministic_stepped, at_ms: 0, step_ms: 1000, for: ["ledger"]}
)
```

A package under `bidamas/` has its own Bluefile. Without one, `blue lock`
counts the package's code as the root's.

```blue file=books/bidamas/ledger/Bluefile
package("ledger", "0.1.0")
```

```blue file=books/bidamas/ledger/ledger.b
def entry(text)
  "#{now_ms} #{text}"
end
```

```blue file=books/main.b
use("ledger", [:entry])

def main()
  write_stdout(unlines([entry("opened"), entry("paid"), entry("closed")]))
end
```

```console
$ blue lock books
books/Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
$ blue run --quiet books/main.b
0 opened
1000 paid
2000 closed
```

Now read the clock in the root itself:

```blue file=books/late.b
use("ledger", [:entry])

def main()
  write_stdout(unlines([entry("opened"), "#{now_ms} closed"]))
end
```

The run refuses it in the check stage, and `blue lock` refuses the project:

```console fails
$ blue run --quiet books/late.b
books/late.b: refused: `now_ms` reaches the host (clock), which this run does not allow; pass --allow clock to grant it
$ blue lock books
blue: [books::main: needs 'clock'] violates ceiling [] (clock is virtualized only for [ledger] and what they use)
```

The other providers are `:seeded_prng` for `:entropy`, and
`:in_memory_overlay` and `:null_sink` for `:filesystem`.
`blue reference` lists each one with its options, under `bluefile`.

---

Source: `docs/howto/test-a-refusal.md`

# Test a refusal

Code says no in three ways: it raises an error of a kind, it returns a
refusal as data, or blue stops a run that reaches past its `--allow`. Each
has its own test.

## An error raised by kind

`raise(:kind, message)` raises. `rescue :kind` catches only that kind.
`tesuto::raises?` tells a test whether a function raises a kind, and
`tesuto::caught` gives the test the error itself:

```blue file=port.b
use("tesuto", %i[caught raises?])

def port(text)
  n = to_int(text)
  if n.nil? or n < 1 or n > 65535
    raise(:bad_option, "port #{text} is not a number from 1 to 65535")
  end
  n
end

def port_or_default(text)
  port(text)
rescue :bad_option
  8080
end

test "a port past 65535 raises :bad_option"
  assert raises?(:bad_option, () -> port("70000"))
end

test "an empty port raises :bad_option"
  assert raises?(:bad_option, () -> port(""))
end

test "the error names the text it refused"
  e = caught(() -> port("http"))
  assert e.kind == :bad_option
  assert e.message == "port http is not a number from 1 to 65535"
end

test "a caller that rescues the kind gets the default"
  assert port_or_default("http") == 8080
  assert port_or_default("443") == 443
end
```

```console
$ blue test port.b
4 test(s): 4 passed, 0 failed
```

## A refusal returned as data

Use `kyohi` when a caller must see every fault, not only the first. A rule
takes the subject and returns a list of refusals, empty when the subject is
sound. `check` runs every rule and returns every refusal. `enforce` is its
raising form: one `:refused` error that carries the refusals as its data.

```blue file=signup.b
use("kyohi", %i[check enforce kinds refusal])
use("tesuto", [:caught])

def named(user)
  if user.name == ""
    [refusal(:blank_name, "a user needs a name")]
  else
    []
  end
end

def adult(user)
  if user.age < 18
    [refusal(:too_young, "#{user.age} is under 18")]
  else
    []
  end
end

def rules()
  [named, adult]
end

test "a sound user has no refusals"
  assert check({name: "ana", age: 30}, rules) == []
end

test "every refusal comes back, not only the first"
  assert kinds(check({name: "", age: 12}, rules)) == %i[blank_name too_young]
end

test "enforce raises one error that carries every refusal"
  e = caught(() -> enforce({name: "", age: 12}, rules))
  assert e.kind == :refused
  assert kinds(e.data) == %i[blank_name too_young]
end
```

```console
$ blue test signup.b
3 test(s): 3 passed, 0 failed
```

## A run that breaches its --allow

A host call in your own file is refused in the check stage, before the run,
and blue exits 1. A host call reached through a package is refused where it
is called. That is a capability breach, and blue exits 77.

Here the `ledger` package reads the clock:

```blue file=Bluefile
package("books", "0.1.0")
packages("bidamas")
```

```blue file=bidamas/ledger/Bluefile
package("ledger", "0.1.0")
```

```blue file=bidamas/ledger/ledger.b
def entry(text)
  "#{now_ms} #{text}"
end
```

```blue file=main.b
use("ledger", [:entry])

def main()
  write_stdout(unlines([entry("opened")]))
end
```

```blue file=direct.b
def main()
  write_stdout(unlines(["#{now_ms} opened"]))
end
```

Held to no capability, the run stops at the call in `ledger`. The error
names the call, the capability and each caller:

```console fails
$ blue run --allow none --quiet main.b
capability breach: `now_ms` reaches the host (clock), which this run's frame does not grant
  at main (main.b:4:25)
```

To test the hold, run blue from the test. `self_exe` is the blue that runs
the test, and `exec_capture` gives its exit status:

```blue file=held.b
use("shisutemu", %i[status_of stderr_of])

def held(file, allow)
  exec_capture(self_exe, "run", "--allow", allow, "--quiet", file)
end

test "the clock reached through ledger breaches a run held to none"
  cap = held("main.b", "none")
  assert status_of(cap) == 77
  assert contains?(stderr_of(cap), "capability breach")
end

test "a clock written in the file is refused before the run"
  assert status_of(held("direct.b", "none")) == 1
end

test "the same run succeeds once it grants the clock"
  assert status_of(held("main.b", "clock")) == 0
end
```

```console
$ blue test held.b
3 test(s): 3 passed, 0 failed
```

---

Source: `docs/howto/pick-a-kernel-hook.md`

# Pick a kernel hook

A hook is where the kernel runs your program. Pick it from what the program must
see, and compile for the kind that hook takes:

| You want to | Hook spec | Program kind | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| decide about a packet first, at the driver | `{xdp: index}` | `:xdp` | an interface index |
| decide about a packet at traffic control | `{tcx_ingress: index}`, `{tcx_egress: index}` | `:sched_cls` | an interface index |
| hold one group of processes to a network rule | `{cgroup_inet_ingress: path}`, `{cgroup_inet_egress: path}` | `:cgroup_skb` | a cgroup directory |
| refuse a socket or a device to a group of processes | `{cgroup_inet_sock_create: path}`, `{cgroup_device: path}` | `:cgroup_sock`, `:cgroup_device` | a cgroup directory |
| decide at a netfilter hook | `{netfilter: {family: :ipv4, hook: :local_in, priority: -100}}` | `:netfilter` | the hook's place |
| count an event the kernel names | `{tracepoint: ["sched", "sched_process_exec"]}`, `{raw_tracepoint: "sched_process_exec"}` | `:tracepoint`, `:raw_tracepoint` | the event |
| watch a kernel function | `{kprobe: name}`, `{fentry: name}`, `{fexit: name}` | `:kprobe`, `:tracing` | the function |
| replace a test function's answer | `{fmod_ret: name}` | `:tracing` | the function |
| deny an operation, such as opening a file | `{lsm: "file_open"}` | `:lsm` | the LSM hook |
| walk kernel objects | `{iter: "task"}` | `:tracing` | the iterator |

`kaaneru::hooks` holds this table as data. Each row's kind is checked here against
it:

```blue file=hooks.b
use("kaaneru", %i[hook_row hooks])
use("retsu", [:size])

def kind_of(spec, kind)
  hook_row({kind:}, spec).kind == kind
end

test "each spec in the table takes the kind the table names"
  assert kind_of({xdp: 1}, :xdp)
  assert kind_of({tcx_ingress: 1}, :sched_cls)
  assert kind_of({tcx_egress: 1}, :sched_cls)
  assert kind_of({cgroup_inet_ingress: "/c"}, :cgroup_skb)
  assert kind_of({cgroup_inet_egress: "/c"}, :cgroup_skb)
  assert kind_of({cgroup_inet_sock_create: "/c"}, :cgroup_sock)
  assert kind_of({cgroup_device: "/c"}, :cgroup_device)
  assert kind_of({netfilter: {}}, :netfilter)
  assert kind_of({tracepoint: ["a", "b"]}, :tracepoint)
  assert kind_of({raw_tracepoint: "a"}, :raw_tracepoint)
  assert kind_of({kprobe: "f"}, :kprobe)
  assert kind_of({fentry: "f"}, :tracing)
  assert kind_of({fexit: "f"}, :tracing)
  assert kind_of({fmod_ret: "f"}, :tracing)
  assert kind_of({lsm: "file_open"}, :lsm)
  assert kind_of({iter: "task"}, :tracing)
end

test "the table is every hook"
  assert size(hooks) == 16
end
```

```console
$ blue test hooks.b
2 test(s): 2 passed, 0 failed
```

Attach with `kaaneru::attached(compiled, spec, body)`. A spec and a kind that do
not fit stop before any call to the kernel, on any host:

```blue file=wrong.b
use("kaaneru", [:attached])

attached({kind: :xdp}, {lsm: "file_open"}, (live) -> live)
```

```console fails
$ blue wrong.b
the lsm hook takes a lsm program, and this one is xdp
```

A spec names one hook, and the refusal lists every hook when it names none or two.

The machine runs a program of any kind that reads its packet or its own memory.
It cannot run a kernel pointer, so a `:netfilter` program that reads the live
`sk_buff` is tested on a real kernel. `BPF_PROG_RUN` refuses `:lsm` with
`ENOTSUPP`, and `kaaneru::run` runs `:tracing` only at the kernel's test functions:
a test of those kinds attaches. Which word and which hook each has run on, with
the test that shows it, is the ledger in [KERNEL.md](docs/KERNEL.md).

Other attachments have their own words, each with a `blue doc` page:
`attach_uprobes`, `attach_kprobes`, `attach_sampling` and `install_struct_ops`.

---

Source: `docs/howto/read-a-kernel-field.md`

# Read a kernel field

`kernel_read(pointer, struct, path, size)` reads one field of a kernel struct.
You name the field. The offset comes from the running kernel's BTF when the program
loads, so the program does not hold an offset that another kernel moved.

```blue file=whoami.b
use("bpf", %i[bind_fields compile helper kernel_read])

def task_pid(_ctx)
  kernel_read(helper(:get_current_task), "task_struct", ["pid"], 4)
end

def program()
  compile("whoami.b", {entry: :task_pid, kind: :tracing, on_fault: 0})
end

def task_at(offset)
  (_struct, _path) -> {offset:, size: 4}
end

test "the program names the field it reads"
  field = program[:fields][0]
  assert field[:struct] == "task_struct"
  assert field[:path] == ["pid"]
end

test "bound to an offset, the program reads the field there"
  memory = {at: 805_306_368, bytes: [0, 0, 0, 0, 42, 0, 0, 0]}
  assert bpf::run(bind_fields(program, task_at(4)), {kernel: memory}).ret == 42
end

test "a read past the struct is the fault answer, never a wrong value"
  memory = {at: 805_306_368, bytes: [1]}
  assert bpf::run(bind_fields(program, task_at(4)), {kernel: memory}).ret == 0
end

test "a field of another size on this kernel refuses to bind"
  other = (_struct, _path) -> {offset: 4, size: 8}
  assert (bind_fields(program, other) rescue :refused) == :refused
end
```

```console
$ blue test whoami.b
4 test(s): 4 passed, 0 failed
```

The tests give the machine a piece of kernel memory and an offset. `bind_fields`
does what a load does: it writes each offset into the program, and it refuses a
field whose size differs from what the program reads.

On a real kernel, `attached` finds the field in this kernel's BTF for you. This
program counts nothing and only reports. It needs Linux and root:

```blue file=watch.b
use("baito", [:bytes_int])
use("bpf", %i[compile declare_map emit helper kernel_read])
use("kaaneru", %i[attached map_named next_event open_events])

EVENTS = declare_map(:events, :ringbuf, 0, 0, 65536)

def on_open(_ctx)
  emit(EVENTS, [kernel_read(helper(:get_current_task), "task_struct", ["pid"], 4)])
  0
end

def main()
  compiled = compile("watch.b", {entry: :on_open, kind: :tracing, on_fault: 0})
  attached(
    compiled,
    {fentry: "do_sys_openat2"},
    fn(live)
      ring = open_events(map_named(live, :events))
      read_file("/proc/version")
      got = next_event(ring, 2000)
      write_stdout(unlines(["a thread opened a file: #{to_s(bytes_int(got, 0, 8) > 0)}"]))
    end
  )
end
```

```console host
$ sudo blue run --allow host --quiet watch.b
a thread opened a file: true
```

A struct or a member this kernel does not have raises `:not_found` at load, and
names it. `blue doc btf::field` shows how to read a field's place by hand.

---

Source: `docs/howto/debug-a-kernel-refusal.md`

# Debug a kernel refusal

Three layers can say no, and each names its error kind. Find the layer first:

| Error kind | Who says it | When |
|---|---|---|
| `:bpf_compile` | blue's compiler | at `compile`, on any host |
| `:bpf_fault` | the pure machine | at `bpf::run`, on any host |
| `:kernel_refused` | the kernel's verifier | at load, on Linux |
| `:kernel_mismatch` | the loader | a field has another size on this kernel |
| `:unsupported` | the host | off Linux, at any word that reaches the kernel |

## The compiler

`:bpf_compile` names the construct. Most refusals come from a value the verifier
would have to bound. Here `*` has operands of unknown range, and the compiler asks
you to bound them or to say that wrapping is what you want:

```blue file=product.b
use("bpf", %i[compile packet_int])

def product(ctx)
  packet_int(ctx, 0, 8) * packet_int(ctx, 8, 8)
end

compile("product.b", {entry: :product, kind: :xdp, on_fault: 0})
```

```console fails
$ blue product.b
bpf_compile
cannot be checked in a kernel program
```

## The machine

`:bpf_fault` means an assembled program did something the machine does not allow.
The machine does not check as much as the verifier does, so this layer finds
faults and does not promise a load:

```blue file=fault.b
use("bpf", %i[assemble exit_program load])

def outside()
  assemble([load(:b, 0, 1, 99999), exit_program])
end

test "a read outside every region is a fault, and the message says where"
  got = begin
    bpf::run(outside)
  rescue :bpf_fault as e
    e.message
  end
  assert contains?(got, "outside every region")
end
```

```console
$ blue test fault.b
1 test(s): 1 passed, 0 failed
```

## The verifier

`:kernel_refused` carries the errno's name and the verifier's whole log as data:
`e.data.name` and `e.data.log`. This program reads a register nothing wrote. It
needs Linux and root:

```blue file=refused.b
use("bpf", %i[alu assemble exit_program r])
use("kaaneru")

def main()
  kaaneru::load(
    assemble([alu(:mov, 0, r(5)), exit_program]),
    {kind: :xdp, name: "refused"}
  )
rescue :kernel_refused as e
  write_stdout(unlines([e.data.name, e.data.log]))
end
```

```console host
$ sudo blue run --allow host --quiet refused.b
EACCES
0: R1=ctx() R10=fp0
0: (bf) r0 = r5
R5 !read_ok
processed 1 insns (limit 1000000) max_states_per_insn 0 total_states 0 peak_states 0 mark_read 0
```

Read the log from the end. The last instruction it names is the one that failed,
and the line after it is the reason. `R5 !read_ok` says that nothing wrote `r5`.
The lines above show what the verifier knew about each register at each step.

To see the instructions by number, print the program:

```blue file=text.b
use("bpf", %i[alu assemble disassemble encode exit_program r])

test "the listing numbers each instruction as the log does"
  listed = disassemble(encode(assemble([alu(:mov, 0, r(5)), exit_program])))
  assert listed == ["r0 = r5", "exit"]
end
```

```console
$ blue test text.b
1 test(s): 1 passed, 0 failed
```

`kernel_absence` says why a host cannot load at all. A test passes it to
`tesuto::skip_for`, so the test is skipped by name and not passed. `BLUE_TEST_SKIP=refuse` turns each skip into a
failure, for a host where every test must run.

---

Source: `docs/howto/ship-a-node-agent.md`

# Ship a node agent

A node agent is a service that loads kernel programs on each node. You declare
the `:kernel_bpf` effect in its `Bluefile`, and blue renders the rest: a DaemonSet,
`CAP_BPF`, `CAP_PERFMON` and `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, and the `bpffs` and `tracefs` mounts.
The rendered chart is checked here. No cluster has run it yet, so test it on yours
first.

```console
$ mkdir agent
$ cd agent
```

```blue file=Bluefile
package("agent", "0.1.0")

service(
  "agent",
  {
    program: "agent.b",
    repository: "ghcr.io/example/agent",
    port: 8080,
    access: {
      effects: %i[network clock entropy environment kernel_bpf],
      host_network: true
    },
    runtime: :native,
    because: :device
  }
)

check("agent", "agent.b")
```

`runtime: :native` with `because: :device` is required: WASI reaches no kernel
ABI. The program answers health checks like any service. Load your kernel program
beside `serve_settings` with the words in
[the first kernel program](docs/tutorial/first-kernel-program.md).

```blue file=agent.b
use("kyuuji")
use("settei")

def handle(req)
  if req[:path] == "/"
    kyuuji::text(200, unlines(["agent"]))
  else
    kyuuji::not_found(req)
  end
end

if settei::serving?
  kyuuji::serve_settings(settei::current, handle)
end

test "the root answers, and anything else is not found"
  assert handle(kyuuji::request("GET", "/", ""))[:status] == 200
  assert handle(kyuuji::request("GET", "/x", ""))[:status] == 404
end
```

```console
$ blue lock .
./Bluefile.lock: 0 source(s) pinned
$ blue test agent.b
1 test(s): 1 passed, 0 failed
```

This program shows what the declaration renders:

```blue file=../show.b
use("haibi", %i[container_security files workload_kind])
use("retsu", [:first])

m = get(json_read(read_file("agent/Bluefile.lock")), "manifest")
spec = get(get(m, "services"), "agent")
paths = map(first, files("agent", get(m, "version"), spec))
write_stdout(unlines(filter((p) -> contains?(p, "daemonset"), paths)))
write_stdout(unlines([workload_kind(spec)]))
write_stdout(unlines(container_security(spec)["capabilities"]["add"]))
```

```console
$ cd ..
$ blue show.b
chart/templates/daemonset.yaml
DaemonSet
BPF
PERFMON
NET_ADMIN
```

`host_network` and `per_node` mean nothing without the effect, so a service that
writes one without `:kernel_bpf` is refused by name when it locks:

```blue file=refused/Bluefile
package("refused", "0.1.0")

service(
  "refused",
  {
    program: "refused.b",
    repository: "ghcr.io/example/refused",
    port: 8080,
    access: {host_network: true}
  }
)
```

```blue file=refused/refused.b
def noop()
  nil
end

test "it passes"
  assert noop.nil?
end
```

```console fails
$ blue lock refused
lacks the :kernel_bpf effect
```

A real agent adds the one-line `flake.nix` that `blue new --kernel` writes. Then
nix builds the image and checks the chart against this shape:

```console host
$ nix flake check
```

`per_node: false` keeps the service a Deployment. The fields are in
[SERVICE-ACCESS.md](docs/SERVICE-ACCESS.md), and which capability each kind of hook
needs is in [KERNEL.md](docs/KERNEL.md) §3.

---

Source: `docs/CANONICAL-FORMS.md`

# Canonical forms

blue has one way to write each thing. This is the inventory of every place where
the surface accepts two or more spellings of one meaning, the spelling blue
writes, why, which layer of the compiler holds it, and the rule that names it.

## The principles, in order

1. **Readability first.** The canonical spelling is the one a person reading the
   line cold understands fastest: words over symbols where blue offers both,
   the descriptive name over the terse one, no clever shorthand. This decided
   every row marked *readability* below. **Amended 2026-10-27
   (`OPERATORS.md` §2):** universal notation is the readable spelling, so a
   symbol wins for indexing, ranges, membership and a science's own operators,
   when the corpus ranks the shape in its top tier or a discipline blue serves
   spells it that way. A rewrite whose safety needs a type fires only at a
   blueshift rung that knows the type; below it the long form stays canonical.
2. **One tree.** Two spellings of one meaning lower to one AST, so every tool
   (the evaluator, the VM, `def_hash`, the checker, the formatter, the LSP)
   sees one shape. Where two spellings built different trees with the same
   meaning, the parser or the resolver now builds the canonical tree.
3. **Corpus frequency** decides only what the first two leave open, measured
   with the parser over the 240 tracked `.b` files of pleme-io on 2026-10-19
   (blue, nix, arnes, substrate, ola-mundo, blackmatter-akeyless, makoto,
   nupastel), aggregated in DuckDB.

## How a rule is held

Every form below still **parses**: an older program, a model or a Ruby habit is
read and means exactly what it says. What it cannot do is stay in a stored
file:

| door | what happens to a non-canonical spelling |
|---|---|
| `blue fmt --write` | writes the canonical spelling |
| `blue run`, `blue test`, `blue check` | refuse a non-canonical entry naming the rules and `blue fmt --write x.b`; they never write a file (`BLUE_LAYOUT=rewrite` restores formatting in place). A loaded dependency is compiled as written: its form is judged by its producer (`BLUE_FORM`, `docs/COMPOUNDING.md`) |
| `blue fmt --check`, a bidama's form check | fail naming the file, the rules and the first place |
| `blue check`, the LSP | report each finding with its code; `blue check --fix` applies the fixes |
| a session, `blue eval`, a string | accepted as written: it has no canonical text to hold |

Two doors decide. The **form door** (`pipeline::form_diagnostics`) compares a
file with its canonical rendering; the parser records which accepted spelling
explains each difference (`blue_lang_syntax::spelling`). The **check stage**
holds what only resolution knows (a builtin's other name, a zero-parameter call)
and the refusals. `blue explain CODE` prints each row.

## The inventory

| written | canonical | why | layer | rule | fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `a && b`, `a \|\| b`, `!x`, `∧ ∨ ¬` | `a and b`, `a or b`, `not x` | readability: read aloud without a lookup; `!` vanishes beside a name. Corpus: 676 `&&`, 333 `\|\|`, 208 `!` | parser (one tree) | B0025 | autofix |
| `unless c` | `if not c` | readability: one conditional keyword; `unless … else` reads backwards. Corpus: 0 | parser | B0026 | autofix |
| `else` holding only `if … end` | `elsif` | one tree; a flat chain, one `end`. Corpus: 2 | parser, formatter | B0027 | autofix (kept when a comment sits beside the inner `if`) |
| `x.f(y)`, `x \|> f(y)` | `f(x, y)` | one tree; the function named first, a recursive call reads forwards. Corpus: 0, 0 | parser | B0028 | autofix |
| `{:a => 1}` | `{a: 1}` | one tree; reads as a field. Corpus: 0 (244 rockets with other keys stay) | parser | B0029 | autofix |
| `def f`, `fn … end` | `def f()`, `fn() … end` | one tree; the definition says it takes nothing | parser | B0030 | autofix |
| `not(x)`, `and(a, b)`, `mod(a, b)`, `equal?(a, b)`, `list(…)`, `define(x, v)`, `0 - x`, `≠ ≤ ≥ × ÷ − ≡` | `not x`, `a and b`, `a % b`, `a == b`, `[…]`, `x = v`, `-x`, the ASCII operator | one tree; readability: the operator a reader can type | parser | B0031 | autofix |
| `[1, 2,]`, `f(a,)`, `{a: 1,}`, `def f(a,)` | no trailing comma | was a parse error; now read and dropped, because models write it | parser | B0032 | autofix |
| `1000000`, `1_000`, `1e3`, a raw control or invisible character in a string | `1_000_000`, `1000`, `1000.0`, `"\u{1b}"` | readability: six or more digits grouped by threes; a character a reader cannot see is never in source (the formatter used to write a raw ESC byte). Corpus: 153 integers of 6+ digits, 6 raw control characters | formatter | B0033 | autofix |
| `not (a == b)`, `not (a != b)` | `a != b`, `a == b` | readability: one comparison; identical by okite D0002. Corpus: 9 | parser (builds `not=`) | B0034 | autofix |
| `{name: name}`, `{:name => name}` | `{name:}` | a label with no value takes the variable of the same name, so a map built from locals names each one once; `{name:, size: 3}` mixes with explicit values. Corpus: 201 entries in 33 files of blue (2026-10-22), 46 files rewritten | parser (reads `{name:}`, notes the long form) | B0046 | autofix |
| `"#{a}\n#{b}"`, `"done\n"`, `"\n"`: a `\n` escape in a string | `join_lines([a, b])`, `unlines(["done"])`, `line_break` | readability: a line break is seen, not counted in escapes; `join_lines` renders each element as interpolation does, so the text is the same (a differential of the old and new binaries, 2026-10-27, byte-identical). A string inside `quote` is data and keeps its escape; `@doc` example text is not rewritten. Corpus: 95 files of blue rewritten (2026-10-27) | parser (one tree) | B0065 | autofix |
| `get(m, :k)`, `get(m, "k")`, `nth(i, xs)`, `nth(0, xs)` | `m[:k]`, `m["k"]`, `xs[i]`, `xs[0]` | universal notation (principle 1, amended): indexing is read without a lookup. One tree: a keyword or string literal key is `get`, any other key `nth`, so a missing key and a position past either end are nil as before. `m.k` is not used for `get`: measured 2026-10-27, `blue-field` raises on a missing field (`errors.rs` `field`), `get` answers nil. A computed map key stays `get(m, k)`. Every bidama's tests byte-identical before and after (77 of 78; tsuiseki differs only in span timestamps and ids). Corpus: 101 files rewritten | parser (one tree) | B0066 | autofix |
| `nil?(x)`, `x == nil`, `nil == x` | `x.nil?` | readability: the test reads as a question put to the value, and one spelling replaces three. `x != nil` and `not x.nil?` stay: the opposite test is its own tree. Each form answers the same on every input class (`blue eval`, 2026-10-23); a map holding a `nil?` key answers `.nil?` with that key. Corpus: 7 `nil?`, the `== nil` tests of every bidama | parser (builds the field read), resolution (`nil?(x)`) | B0047 | autofix |
